#How human works

flow 1 · decompile

  you      ask for a file: /decompile src/app.py
  claude   reads the file and picks the shape from the kind of file,
           by [the decompile skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/decompile/SKILL.md) and
           [the shape catalog](compiler/cli/human/shapes/README.md): one run takes the rail,
           a set of functions the sections, a dispatcher the desk, a rulebook the dialogue.
  claude   writes the telling for [a reader who does not read code](compiler/cli/human/skills/decompile/SKILL.md:e1:explain),
           with pins on the words that name a thing. Every other word is free.
  claude   shows the text and stops — even when your message sounded like approval.
  you      [say the word: map it.](e3:the word)
  claude   pipes the exact text into [human map](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:cmd_map).
  tool     gates the entry, no claude call: [every pin points at a real thing](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:build_anchors),
           no two pins share their words, [no circle](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:check_cycle),
           and each block pin gets [its exact lines](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:block_spans).
           A refusal is the gate speaking: claude reads it, fixes the text, runs again.
           Words you wrote yourself go in with --verbatim: plain, kept as yours,
           [and a pin in them refused](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:verbatim_record) — the pins come after, with retext;
           a copy of them stays beside the entry as the origin, so a later mending can be measured against it.
  disk     one entry appended to human/explanation_<path>.json, never one changed.
  claude   [reports](compiler/cli/human/skills/decompile/SKILL.md:e1:report): the entry, its pins, the coverage,
           the warnings of [human show](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:cmd_show) — and offers the next telling:
           a zoom on one block, a plainer layer over the whole, or [the project itself](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:cmd_map_project),
           whose pins reach the files and the entries of their maps.


flow 2 · compile

  you      give an abstraction: /human an http server that returns hello world
  claude   follows [the human skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md): [the run](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md:e1:the run)
           registers the project first, and your words reach the tool before any code is written.
  tool     [human init](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the register) registers the project: [sweeps the tree](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the sweep)
           through [the ignore sieve](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the sieve), writes the file list into human/human.json,
           copies the reader in, and starts the empty project map.
  claude   hands your words to the project map as they are — human map project --verbatim —
           no spelling fixed, no word trimmed. [the verbatim gate](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the guard) refuses
           a pin in them: the pins come later, when the things they point at exist. The entry is
           flagged as yours and keeps that first copy as its origin.
  claude   writes the code files, no comments. The gate is static like a compiler's: the file must parse.
  claude   maps the detailed telling of each file — entry 1, a catalog shape, pins into the blocks.
  claude   hands your words back with the pins inserted, through a plain retext of that entry:
           [the gate strips the pins out](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the gate on your words) and compares the rest
           with the words it holds, character for character.
           A changed word is a refusal. Pins go in; your words never change on this road.
  you      reword them later on your own word: human retext project <id> --verbatim takes new words,
           resets the origin, and marks stale the entries that stood on the old words;
           a sync rewords them only when the code forces it, and says so.
  claude   reports, serves, and arms the watch, so what you write in the reader reaches it — flow 8.
           Afterwards you correct with retext, undo, sync — the commands of flow 1.


flow 3 · read

  you      start the reader from anywhere in the project: human serve
  tool     [climbs to the folder that holds human/human.json](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:find_root) and [serves it](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the shelf),
           printing the localhost line, [the tailnet line](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:tailnet address), the line that says
           an open training session shows as a layer over the reader, the line that says a new file
           from the reader lands next to the others, and the line
           that says a writing in the reader lands in human/server/ — flow 8.
  tool     answers human.json with [a live file list](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:rebuilt) — a fresh sweep on every ask,
           so a deleted file leaves the tree and a new one appears, no init, no restart.
  you      open [the reader](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html): human.json opens first, project.json stands under it;
           a file shows [every entry as one folded header](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:render), the most detailed first;
           a click on a pin [jumps to its entry](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:jump), and a pin into another file
           [switches file](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:crossJump) — a project pin lands on the entry and lights the anchor.


flow 4 · sync — the code changed

  you      change the code, then: human sync src/app.py
  tool     [a deterministic pass](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:cmd_sync), no claude: [maps every old line to its new line](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the line map),
           [re-resolves every pin and every span](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the re-resolving). Lines that only moved end here.
  tool     finds the entries the change touches: lines changed, a pin broken, new lines inside the block.
  tool     writes the letter to claude: the file and its absolute path — read the whole file —, the diff,
           [the project files it imports](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the line about the neighbours), the blocks, the entries to mend, the rules:
           keep the untouched lines, keep every anchor, add a sentence for each behaviour the change added.
           An entry of your own words goes in [named as yours](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the mark on your words),
           and the rules ask for the smallest edit, in your voice.
  claude   [answers with the mended texts](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:ask_claude), run at the project root,
           the letter given through the pipe and never on the command line, so a long one is not cut short.
  tool     [gates the answer on a copy](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the rebuild), up to --tries times: every block exists,
           every anchor kept, every needed word alive. Four failures leave the map untouched.
  disk     the map saved; the entries that point into a mended one marked stale — in the file's map,
           and in the project map when a project entry pins the mended one — when a word changed,
           never when the pins alone moved.
           A warning when [new lines landed inside an entry](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the pieces the new lines fall in) and no word changed.
           A warning too when [the sync moved words of your own](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the word when your words moved):
           the first copy stays in the map, and human show marks the entry with
           [the line that brings them back](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the word about your words).
  you      for the whole project: human sync project. The old state is git HEAD; the tool asks git for
           [the files that changed](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:changed_files), re-resolves the file, block, and entry pins,
           and [sends one letter](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:cmd_sync) for the entries that pin a changed file.
           A project entry of your own words goes in named as yours there too, and the same warning
           follows when the answer moved them.


flow 5 · carry down — a parent telling changed

  disk     entry 1 changed — by a sync or a retext — and entry 2 points into it,
           so [entry 2 is marked stale](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:mark_children) with a copy of the old text.
           The mark is a list: a second changed parent adds [a note of its own](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:add_note),
           and a parent that changes twice before the repair keeps its first old text — the versions
           between are the base of nothing. A retext of entry 2 does not take the mark off; only the
           repair does, so the tool knows the mending happened and was not guessed.
  you      ask for the repair: human sync src/app.py --stale 2
  tool     writes the second letter: one page for each changed parent — its old text, its new text, the
           diff between the two — then the dependent's text,
           the rules: mend the words that went wrong, keep every anchor and [every word another entry needs](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:needed_words),
           carry a new fact down at the dependent's own level, pinned at the parent's new anchor.
           When the dependent holds words of your own, the letter asks for the smallest edit, in your voice.
           A parent that is gone stops the run.
  claude   answers with the mended dependent — words only, never code.
  tool     [gates and saves](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:repair_stale); the dependents of entry 2 are marked stale in turn.
           A repair that moved words of your own is named on the spot, as a sync's is.
           A parent's child can be a parent: the next layer waits for your next word, one layer at a time.
           A project entry made stale by a file's entry is repaired the same way, each note naming its
           file, with the parent read from that file's map: [human sync project --stale](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:repair_stale).


flow 6 · train — the catalog learns from real picks

  you      give this machine its key once: human login <key> — [the sessions live in a store](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the store hand)
           away from your disk, and without the key the training refuses and says to log in.
  you      open a session: human train --open. [Rows without a pick carry over](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:carry).
           A write in the reader that asks claude for a telling — a decompile, a create, an expansion
           with no words — [opens one by itself](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:the training of an ask) when none is open.
  claude   on the next /decompile or sync, or the next such ask of the reader, writes two or three versions per file instead of one:
           best — the catalog shape, with --shape; refinement — for a sync row only, the map's own text,
           filled by the tool, and refused on a new telling, which holds best and free and shows two
           cards in the layer; free — no shape rule. [Each version goes in with its own call](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:cmd_add),
           passes the same pin gates as a map — [the anchors the project map pins into the entry](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the anchors the project map pins into it)
           among the ones it must keep — and a rewrite keeps its earlier text in the history.
           Each call answers with [the slots filled](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the slots filled) and,
           on its own line, [the slots still empty](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the slots still empty), so
           claude writes the missing one before it reports to you.
           An expansion goes in with the entry it hangs from and the highlighted words, one row for each
           such entry, and its versions may not pin into that entry.
  tool     keeps an open row current when the entry it studies is retexted — in a file's map or the
           project's, by you or by a sync: a row is a photo of its entry, and
           [the row follows](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:refresh_row) with a second photo —
           the copy of the entry's text it keeps becomes the new words, and a middle card that
           still held the old text takes the new one and keeps the old as v1. A middle already
           rewritten stays as it is, and the layer stops calling it current. A store that does not
           answer only warns here: the retext itself stands.
  tool     serves [the feed](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:loadTrain) as a layer over the reader: an open session covers the page
           on its own, hide puts it away, a line in the bar with the counts brings it back, and so does a new row.
           The session list — from the store — and the fresh map come as JSON;
           [a pick lands in the open session](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:pick) over POST, no restart.
  you      swipe and pick — sideways for the versions, up for the next row — and leave a comment if you want.
  you      close: human train --close, or the close training button of the layer, which first says what the close will do.
  tool     gives a new telling with no pick [a version of its own](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:takes a version of its own) — best, or free
           when best is missing — and marks the pick as a default, so a write from the reader always lands.
           A sync row with no pick, or a row that misses its versions, is named and carries over.
  tool     [applies each pick](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:apply_row) as a retext of the entry or a new map, then [marks the session finished](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:cmd_close).
           The maps never change before the close. A pick that rewords an entry the project map points
           at leaves a stale note there, one for each changed parent. When an expansion lands,
           [a link event](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the pin of its target into the new entry) waits for claude, so the highlighted words
           of the entry it hangs from are pinned down into it.
  store    one session record under your name, never a file on your disk: the rows, the versions with
           their shape and history, the pick, the comment, and a copy of the code — or, for the
           project, [of every file](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:snapshot).


flow 7 · shapes — how the catalog changes

  claude   reads the finished sessions: which slot won, which shape it wore, what the comment said.
  claude   tells you what it learned and the fix it would make, by [the shapes skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/shapes/SKILL.md):
           [the smallest change that would have produced the ideal](compiler/cli/human/skills/shapes/SKILL.md:e1:the comparison) —
           a new shape, a rule added or changed, or the example changed.
  you      [validate, or not](compiler/cli/human/skills/shapes/SKILL.md:e1:the validation). Without the word, the catalog does not change.
  claude   edits shapes/<shape>.md, bumps the version, reinstalls, and redeploys with [human skills](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the giver).
           The next /decompile reads the new rule.


flow 8 · write in the reader — your words come from the page, not the terminal

  you      click the text of an entry: a box opens in its place, the raw text, pins and all — the same
           text retext takes — with the caret where you clicked, and it grows as you type. A file with
           no map shows one place for its telling and the code of the file under it, and the bar says
           there is no abstraction yet; an empty project map offers a new abstraction, and once a map
           holds an entry that place is gone. Escape, or a click away, closes the box and keeps what
           you wrote — only the box now open answers a click away;
           a click on a pin jumps and opens no box. A pin you just typed, one the map does not hold yet,
           [is read from the target it names](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:guessAnchor).
           A pin the page cannot follow shows that target beside the words, and the caret counts past
           the shown name, so a click after such a pin still lands where you clicked.
           Typing keeps nothing: Ctrl+S puts the draft in the browser, and the bar says unsaved until you press it.
           Your words [stay in the place you wrote them](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:keepBox) when the page
           draws again between one box and the next.
           The page keeps its place through all of it: the box opens, grows and closes where you were reading,
           and an empty place for a telling lights under the pointer, so you see it can be written in.
  you      make a file from the page: the new file line at the top of the file tree takes a path from the
           root, folders and all, and [the server makes the file empty](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the new file), so it opens on its new abstraction
           and the code comes under your words. No event is queued. A path out of the project, into human/,
           or onto a file already there is refused, with the reason. The tree follows the files on disk,
           so a file claude makes shows without a reload. Git holds no old copy of a file made here,
           so its first sync runs against an empty old version.
  you      ask for a telling you do not write yourself, by three roads: on a file with no map the open
           place carries a decompile button — not on an empty file, whose words come first — and one
           click asks claude for the whole-file telling;
           on a mapped entry you highlight words and right-click for expand abstraction, which opens a
           write place on top whose head is the button — your words there, or none at all; a right-click
           on the head of an entry gives create abstraction, a plainer telling over that entry, nothing
           to write. These three send themselves at the click and wait for no compile button, and each
           opens from [the little menu of a right click](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:the menu).
           An expansion is a deeper telling of the words you highlighted: it stands above the entry,
           and the entry pins those words down into it, as a zoom on one block stands above the
           telling of the whole file.
  you      take an entry away: the same right-click on its head offers delete abstraction, and
           [the head turns into the button](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:to take that one away), with a cancel beside it.
           One click takes the entry out at once — this road waits for no compile button and queues
           no event, because nothing is left for claude to do.
  tool     runs human undo <name> --entry <id>, and [the gate refuses it](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the gate)
           while another entry, the project map, or an open training row still stands on that entry.
           [The open row comes over the network](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the training store): a machine with
           no key goes through without that last look, and a store that does not answer stops the undo.
  you      press the compile button, which stands in the bar while a text differs from the map:
           [it sends every place you changed](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:compile), one after the other. The map changes only then.
  tool     takes the writing at the door — [its body read as JSON](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the body) —
           and [runs the command you would have typed](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:the command run), one per changed text:
           an entry rewritten goes in as human retext <name> <id> --verbatim, a first telling as
           human map <name> --verbatim, and code on a file with no map is written to the file.
           An expansion you wrote words for goes in the same way, as human map <name> --verbatim, so the
           map holds your words before claude works; an expansion with no words, a decompile and a
           create map nothing at the click — the event alone waits. On a machine with a key and a store
           that answers, that event names the open training session, one opened for it when none was — flow 6.
           A file under human/ is refused — the maps take no writing.
           The gates are the ones of flow 1: a refusal comes back to the page in the command's own
           words, named by the place it came from, and nothing is queued.
  disk     one event appended to human/server/events.jsonl: the kind, the name, the paths of the map and
           the file, the entry, the old text and the new, and for a code write
           [the pins that reach the file](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:the pins that reach a file).
           An expansion and a create name the entry they stand on, and an expansion carries the
           highlighted words with their pins.
  you      arm the listening once, from the project root: human watch.
  tool     [prints every event claude has not finished](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:cmd_watch), one JSON line each, then
           follows the queue; --once prints what waits now and returns. An event printed in an earlier
           session comes back marked replay, so claude reads the maps before it syncs anything.
  claude   takes them in order, by [the writing part of the human skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md:e1:the writing):
           reads the diff of your words, writes the code they ask for — in a new file when no file of the
           project holds that thing —, syncs every map that stood on
           them, and pins the new sentences back in. A decompile, a create, or an expansion with no
           words has no text of yours to read: claude writes that telling itself and maps it — or, when
           the event names a training session, writes it twice into a row, maps nothing, and the close
           of flow 6 maps your pick. A link event from that close asks only for the last step of an
           expansion: the highlighted words of the entry pinned down into the new one.
           Then [human ack <number>](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:cmd_ack) — the queue
           advances and says how many are left.
  you      see the wait in the page: the entry is marked compiling until the ack, because the reader
           [asks every three seconds](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:pollQueue) and the door answers with
           [what still waits](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:pending). When the wait ends, the page reads
           that map again, so the new words show, and the training looks again for new rows.

           and sends one letter for the entries that pin a changed file.
           A project entry of your own words goes in named as yours there too, and the same warning
           follows when the answer moved them.


flow 5 · carry down — a parent telling changed

  disk     entry 1 changed — by a sync or a retext — and entry 2 points into it,
           so entry 2 is marked stale with a copy of the old text.
           The mark is a list: a second changed parent adds a note of its own,
           and a parent that changes twice before the repair keeps its first old text — the versions
           between are the base of nothing. A retext of entry 2 does not take the mark off; only the
           repair does, so the tool knows the mending happened and was not guessed.
  you      ask for the repair: human sync src/app.py --stale 2
  tool     writes the second letter: one page for each changed parent — its old text, its new text, the
           diff between the two — then the dependent's text,
           the rules: mend the words that went wrong, keep every anchor and every word another entry needs,
           carry a new fact down at the dependent's own level, pinned at the parent's new anchor.
           When the dependent holds words of your own, the letter asks for the smallest edit, in your voice.
           A parent that is gone stops the run.
  claude   answers with the mended dependent — words only, never code.
  tool     gates and saves; the dependents of entry 2 are marked stale in turn.
           A repair that moved words of your own is named on the spot, as a sync's is.
           A parent's child can be a parent: the next layer waits for your next word, one layer at a time.
           A project entry made stale by a file's entry is repaired the same way, each note naming its
           file, with the parent read from that file's map: human sync project --stale.


flow 6 · train — the catalog learns from real picks

  you      open a session: human train --open. Rows without a pick carry over.
  claude   on the next /decompile or sync, writes two or three versions per file instead of one:
           best — the catalog shape, with --shape; refinement — for a sync row only, the map's own text,
           filled by the tool, and refused on a new telling, which holds best and free and shows two
           cards in the feed; free — no shape rule. Each version goes in with its own call,
           passes the same pin gates as a map — the anchors the project map pins into the entry
           among the ones it must keep — and a rewrite keeps its earlier text in the history.
           Each call answers with the slots filled and,
           on its own line, the slots still empty, so
           claude writes the missing one before it reports to you.
  tool     keeps an open row current when the entry it studies is retexted — in a file's map or the
           project's, by you or by a sync: a row is a photo of its entry, and
           the row follows with a second photo —
           the copy of the entry's text it keeps becomes the new words, and a middle card that
           still held the old text takes the new one and keeps the old as v1. A middle already
           rewritten stays as it is, and the feed stops calling it current.
  tool     serves the feed: the session list and the fresh map come as JSON;
           a pick lands in the open session over POST, no restart.
  you      swipe and pick — sideways for the versions, down for the next file — and leave a comment if you want.
  you      close: human train --close.
  tool     names every row not yet applied that still misses a version, so an unfinished row is seen
           before the applying starts.
  tool     applies each pick as a retext of the entry or a new map, then marks the session finished.
           The maps never change before the close. A pick that rewords an entry the project map points
           at leaves a stale note there, one for each changed parent.
  disk     human/training/<session>.json: the rows, the versions with their shape and history,
           the pick, the comment, and a copy of the code — or, for the project, of every file.


flow 7 · shapes — how the catalog changes

  claude   reads the finished sessions: which slot won, which shape it wore, what the comment said.
  claude   tells you what it learned and the fix it would make, by the shapes skill:
           the smallest change that would have produced the ideal —
           a new shape, a rule added or changed, or the example changed.
  you      validate, or not. Without the word, the catalog does not change.
  claude   edits shapes/<shape>.md, bumps the version, reinstalls, and redeploys with human skills.
           The next /decompile reads the new rule.


flow 8 · write in the reader — your words come from the page, not the terminal

  you      click the text of an entry: a box opens in its place, the raw text, pins and all — the same
           text retext takes — with the caret where you clicked, and it grows as you type. A file with
           no map shows one place for its telling and the code of the file under it, and the bar says
           there is no abstraction yet; an empty project map offers a new abstraction, and once a map
           holds an entry that place is gone. Escape, or a click away, closes the box and keeps what
           you wrote — only the box now open answers a click away;
           a click on a pin jumps and opens no box. A pin you just typed, one the map does not hold yet,
           is read from the target it names.
           A pin the page cannot follow shows that target beside the words, and the caret counts past
           the shown name, so a click after such a pin still lands where you clicked.
           Typing keeps nothing: Ctrl+S puts the draft in the browser, and the bar says unsaved until you press it.
           Your words stay in the place you wrote them when the page
           draws again between one box and the next.
           The page keeps its place through all of it: the box opens, grows and closes where you were reading,
           and an empty place for a telling lights under the pointer, so you see it can be written in.
  you      ask for a telling you do not write yourself, by three roads: on a file with no map the open
           place carries a decompile button, and one click asks claude for the whole-file telling;
           on a mapped entry you highlight words and right-click for expand abstraction, which opens a
           write place on top whose head is the button — your words there, or none at all; a right-click
           on the head of an entry gives create abstraction, a plainer telling over that entry, nothing
           to write. These three send themselves at the click and wait for no compile button, and each
           opens from the little menu of a right click.
           An expansion is a deeper telling of the words you highlighted: it stands above the entry,
           and the entry pins those words down into it, as a zoom on one block stands above the
           telling of the whole file.
  you      press the compile button, which stands in the bar while a text differs from the map:
           it sends every place you changed, one after the other. The map changes only then.
  tool     takes the writing at the door — its body read as JSON —
           and runs the command you would have typed, one per changed text:
           an entry rewritten goes in as human retext <name> <id> --verbatim, a first telling as
           human map <name> --verbatim, and code on a file with no map is written to the file.
           An expansion you wrote words for goes in the same way, as human map <name> --verbatim, so the
           map holds your words before claude works; an expansion with no words, a decompile and a
           create map nothing at the click — the event alone waits.
           A file under human/ is refused — the maps take no writing.
           The gates are the ones of flow 1: a refusal comes back to the page in the command's own
           words, named by the place it came from, and nothing is queued.
  disk     one event appended to human/server/events.jsonl: the kind, the name, the paths of the map and
           the file, the entry, the old text and the new, and for a code write
           the pins that reach the file.
           An expansion and a create name the entry they stand on, and an expansion carries the
           highlighted words with their pins.
  you      arm the listening once, from the project root: human watch.
  tool     prints every event claude has not finished, one JSON line each, then
           follows the queue; --once prints what waits now and returns. An event printed in an earlier
           session comes back marked replay, so claude reads the maps before it syncs anything.
  claude   takes them in order, by the writing part of the human skill:
           reads the diff of your words, writes the code they ask for, syncs every map that stood on
           them, and pins the new sentences back in. A decompile, a create, or an expansion with no
           words has no text of yours to read: claude writes that telling itself and maps it.
           Then human ack <number> — the queue
           advances and says how many are left.
  you      see the wait in the page: the entry is marked compiling until the ack, because the reader
           asks every three seconds and the door answers with
           what still waits.

explanations.text:
"map it" — what happens between your word and the entry on disk

●  you say the word                                            ([the word](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:cmd_map))
  │     Claude has shown the story and waited. "map it" is the only word that moves it:
  │     the text goes to the tool exactly as shown, through the pipe, with the name of the
  │     file and, for a zoom, the name of the piece it tells.
  │
  ●  the tool reads the file and finds its pieces                ([the pieces of the file](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:block_spans))
  │     It opens the code and notes every named piece with its first and its last line.
  │     It does this for one reason: so a pin on a piece can be given its exact lines.
  │
  ●  the tool reads the pins out of the story                    ([the reading of the pins](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:build_anchors))
  │     Every pair of bracketed words with a target after them is one pin. The target must be
  │     a real piece of the file, an anchor of an earlier story, or a file of the project;
  │     a dead name stops the run. Two pins may not share their words, and
  │     no pin may make a circle back to the story it stands in.
  │
  ●  the tool guards your own words                              ([the guard on your words](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:verbatim_record))
  │     When the text is yours, given with --verbatim, a pin in it is refused: your words go in
  │     plain, and the pins come later, with retext. A copy stays beside the entry as the origin,
  │     so a later mending can be measured against it.
  │
  ●  the tool writes one entry and never changes another         ([the record](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:the record))
  │     The entry gets the next number, the text, the pins with their exact lines,
  │     and the lines of the piece it tells. It is appended to the map of the file;
  │     the entries before it stay as they were.
  │
  ●  the tool answers you                                        ([the answer](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:counts the lines no abstraction points at yet))
        One line for the entry — its number, its piece, how many pins — and one for the coverage:
        how many lines of code a story now points at. When a check failed, a refusal comes
        instead, in the words of the check, so claude fixes the text and says the word again.

anchors.anchor: counts the lines no abstraction points at yet
